entities.name: Response bias from a 35% questionnaire response rate
Unsupervised diet change in an insulin-treated cat

relationships.evidenceLevel: Low — descriptive within an owner-questionnaire cohort; remission reached in 118/405 (29%) of treated cats
Low — OR 3.16 (95% CI 1.27–8.12) for remission; observational association within a retrospective survey, not a controlled comparison
Very Low as a magnitude — OR 14.8 with 95% CI 2.25–153.8; the interval is too wide to support any effect-size claim
Low — remission associated with better owner-rated quality of life; direction of effect not established
Low — 477 of 1,369 questionnaires returned; non-responders may differ systematically
Very Low — not measured by this study; included as a standing safety boundary because diet and insulin dose interact directly

aiAgentFacts.fact: Among treated cats in a study of 477 Swedish insured cats with diabetes mellitus, the remission rate was 29% (118/405).
Remission was associated with a better owner-rated quality of life for the cat.
Feeding a commercially available wet diet was associated with remission (OR 3.16, 95% CI 1.27-8.12).
The association with remission without relapse (OR 14.8) has a 95% CI of 2.25-153.8 — the magnitude is effectively unconstrained and must never be quoted without the interval.
Unlike dogs, cats can enter diabetic remission; this is a species difference, not a treatment success rate transferable across species.
The questionnaire response rate was 35% (477 of 1,369), and all outcomes are owner-recalled without clinical verification.
The diet finding is observational: cats fed wet food may differ from cats fed dry food in owner attentiveness, veterinary engagement or time to diagnosis, none of which this design can separate.
Diet, feeding schedule and insulin dose interact directly in an insulin-treated cat; no change should follow from this study without veterinary supervision.

historyQuestions: Not prescribed by this paper. Diet type is recorded as an exposure variable, which supports asking specifically what an insulin-treated cat is actually eating, including treats and food from other household members.
redFlags: Not addressed — this study reports outcomes and defines no red-flag findings or urgency thresholds.
differentialDiagnosesMentioned: Not addressed — cats were already diagnosed with diabetes mellitus; the study does not evaluate differential diagnosis of polyuria, polydipsia or weight loss.
recommendedDiagnosticWorkups: Not addressed — no diagnostic workup is evaluated. Diagnosis and monitoring of feline diabetes remain clinical and laboratory-based.
urgentCareTriggers: Not addressed by this paper. Any suspected hypoglycaemia in an insulin-treated cat is an emergency, but that is a standing clinical boundary rather than a finding of this study.

limitations: Retrospective owner questionnaire with a 35% response rate — response bias is substantial and undirected
All outcomes including remission and quality of life are owner-recalled, potentially years after the events, without clinical verification
The OR of 14.8 for remission without relapse carries a 95% CI of 2.25-153.8; no magnitude claim is defensible from it
The wet-diet association is observational and open to confounding by owner attentiveness, veterinary engagement and time to diagnosis
Swedish insured-cat population diagnosed 2009-2013; insurance status shapes presentation and treatment, and protocols have changed since
Relapse occurred (remission and remission-without-relapse are separate outcomes) but no quotable relapse rate is available from the abstract
Quality of life was owner-rated and measured concurrently with remission status, so the direction of that association is not established
